reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of intestinal zinc uptake caused by SLC39A4 variants affecting the ZIP4 transporter
Classic triad is periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia and diarrhoea, often emerging when breast-feeding is stopped
Skin lesions are sharply demarcated, scaly, erythematous or vesiculobullous around the mouth, nappy area and over the hands and feet
Associated features include irritability, poor growth, recurrent infections and impaired wound healing
A low serum zinc with reduced alkaline phosphatase (a zinc-dependent enzyme) supports the diagnosis
Acquired zinc deficiency from inadequate intake or malabsorption can mimic the inherited disorder and must be considered
Skin, gut and growth abnormalities respond rapidly and dramatically to zinc replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by variants in SLC39A4, which encodes the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 responsible for zinc uptake at the enterocyte apical membrane. Impaired transport leads to systemic zinc deficiency. Zinc is a cofactor for numerous metalloenzymes and is essential for epithelial integrity, immune function and cell proliferation, so its deficiency produces the characteristic dermatitis at sites of friction and around orifices, hair loss, impaired healing and immune dysfunction, together with malabsorptive diarrhoea. Because human milk contains a zinc-binding ligand that aids absorption, symptoms often surface after weaning from breast milk.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired zinc deficiency from poor intake, malabsorption or parenteral nutrition
Epidermolysis bullosa and other blistering skin disorders
Candidiasis and seborrhoeic or atopic dermatitis
additionalInvestigations: Serum zinc concentration, ideally in a zinc-free container to avoid contamination
Serum alkaline phosphatase as a zinc-dependent enzyme marker
Molecular genetic testing for SLC39A4 variants to distinguish inherited from acquired deficiency
Dietary and nutritional assessment for causes of acquired deficiency
Skin examination and, where uncertain, biopsy to characterise the dermatitis
redFlags: Extensive erosive or secondarily infected skin disease
Severe failure to thrive and immune compromise with recurrent infections
Rapid clinical deterioration in an untreated infant
Persistent symptoms despite replacement suggesting non-adherence or an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The inherited form requires lifelong zinc replacement but carries an excellent prognosis once treatment is established, with rapid resolution of skin, gastrointestinal and growth abnormalities. Untreated disease can be life-threatening.
pitfalls: Not distinguishing inherited ZIP4 deficiency from acquired zinc deficiency, which alters duration of treatment
Falsely low or high zinc levels from sample contamination or handling
Misdiagnosing the rash as candidiasis or eczema and delaying zinc therapy
Stopping zinc prematurely in the genetic form, allowing relapse
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Lifelong oral zinc replacement (zinc sulphate, gluconate or acetate), which rapidly reverses the dermatitis, alopecia and diarrhoea
Monitor serum zinc, alkaline phosphatase and growth to titrate replacement
Watch for copper deficiency arising from excessive zinc supplementation
Distinguish the inherited disorder from acquired zinc deficiency and address any dietary or malabsorptive cause
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive SLC39A4 inheritance
